# Designing slides

The rest of this part of the book is about the figure: the theme, the colors,
the legend, the saved file. This chapter steps back to the slide the figure
lands on, and to the people in the room reading it while you talk. There is no
code here. The recipes for building a slide-ready plot are in
[slides and presentations](presentations.qmd); this chapter is the reasoning
behind them.

The short version: state each finding as a one-sentence headline, show the
evidence as a figure, and remove everything else.

## When to use it

Read this before you build a deck, not after. Most of what goes wrong on a
clinical slide is decided when the talk is planned (a topic title, six bullets,
a table pasted from the manuscript) and no theme argument fixes it later.

It is also the place to settle an argument. Each recommendation below names
the study, standard or experience it rests on, so "the guidelines say so" can
be checked rather than taken on trust.

## The central principle

A slide is not a document projected on a wall. The speaker, the slide and the
audience work as one system, so we design them together. Ask one question of
every slide: what work is this asking the audience to do?

A manuscript figure has a reader who can stop, go back and read the legend
twice. A slide has a listener who hears the talk once, in order, while you keep
talking. Everything that follows comes from taking that difference seriously.

## How audiences process slides

An audience holds only about four chunks in working memory at once
[@Cowan:2001], so every element on a slide competes with what you are saying.
Mayer and Fiorella's review of controlled experiments [@MayerFiorella:2014] and
Mayer and Pilegard's companion review [@MayerPilegard:2014] give eight design
rules that cut this load.

| Principle | What to do on a slide | Tests supporting it | Median effect size (d) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Temporal contiguity | Show the figure while you talk about it, not before or after | 9 of 9 | 1.22 |
| Spatial contiguity | Put labels on or beside what they describe, not in a legend or footnote | 22 of 22 | 1.10 |
| Coherence | Remove decoration, logos, background images and side facts | 23 of 23 | 0.86 |
| Redundancy | Don't put your spoken sentences on screen as text; show the graphic and say the words | 16 of 16 | 0.86 |
| Segmenting | Break a complex figure or process into steps and build it up | 10 of 10 | 0.79 |
| Modality | Explain a figure in speech rather than in printed text beside it | 53 of 61 | 0.76 |
| Pre-training | Define key terms, groups and abbreviations before the results that use them | 13 of 16 | 0.75 |
| Signaling | Cue structure: headline, highlight the series or number that matters, section dividers | 24 of 28 | 0.41 |

: Eight multimedia-learning principles, the slide practice each implies, and the evidence behind it. {#tbl-slide-mayer}

The two contiguity principles, coherence, redundancy and signaling are from
Mayer and Fiorella; segmenting, modality and pre-training are from Mayer and
Pilegard.

Two caveats before you lean on those numbers. Most of these experiments tested
students learning unfamiliar material, and none tested clinical conference
audiences specifically. And the segmenting experiments let learners set the
pace; in a talk, the speaker sets it.

## Slide structure: assertion-evidence

Replace the topic title and bullet list with a one-sentence headline that
states the finding, supported by a figure. Garner and Alley tested this
directly [@GarnerAlley:2013]. 110 engineering students heard the same recorded
talk with either default topic-and-bullet slides or assertion-evidence slides.
The assertion-evidence group showed better comprehension, fewer
misconceptions, lower perceived cognitive load and stronger recall a week
later.

On a slide that works out as follows.

- **Headline.** A short full sentence that states the result: "[Exposure]
  doubled [outcome] at 30 days", not "[Exposure] and [outcome]".
- **Body.** A figure, image or diagram as the evidence. Text only where a
  figure can't carry it.
- **One task at a time.** Give the audience one coherent task per visual
  state. Several ideas can share a slide when the relationship between them is
  the point; when you need two headlines, you need two slides.
- **Signals.** Use the headline, a highlighted series or an arrow to point at
  what matters, rather than making the audience search.
- **Self-contained slides.** Don't make the audience remember an earlier slide
  to read this one. Repeat the key number, group name or definition, since
  working memory holds about four chunks.
- **Text when it earns its place.** A quotation, a definition or eligibility
  criteria the audience must inspect can carry real text. Show it and pause, or
  point to the line; don't read it aloud over the audience reading it
  (redundancy). The problem is a competing verbal channel, not word count.

Examples and templates are at
[assertion-evidence.com](https://www.assertion-evidence.com/).

## Color and accessibility

WCAG 2.2 sets the contrast thresholds we hold slides to [@WCAG22:2023]: 4.5:1
for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18 pt, or 14 pt bold), and 3:1 for the
chart elements a viewer needs to read the data. About 1 in 12 men have a color
vision deficiency, most often red-green
([National Eye Institute](https://www.nei.nih.gov/learn-about-eye-health/eye-conditions-and-diseases/color-blindness)),
so in a room of 100 clinicians several will not see a red-green contrast.

For data series, use the Okabe-Ito color-vision-safe palette [@OkabeIto:CUD],
which is built into R as `palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")` and is the
source of `hv_ppt_palette()`. The light ordering there swaps orange for a
darkened yellow so that all six colors clear 3:1 on white (see
[colors](colors.qmd)). Color-vision-safe is not the same as high contrast,
though. On white, only some of the stock colors reach 3:1.

| Okabe-Ito color | Hex | Contrast on white |
|---|---|---|
| Blue | `#0072B2` | 5.19:1 |
| Vermilion | `#D55E00` | 3.87:1 |
| Bluish green | `#009E73` | 3.42:1 |
| Reddish purple | `#CC79A7` | 3.06:1 |
| Orange | `#E69F00` | 2.25:1 |
| Sky blue | `#56B4E9` | 2.31:1 |
| Yellow | `#F0E442` | 1.32:1 |

: Contrast of each Okabe-Ito color against a white background, computed with the WCAG relative-luminance formula. {#tbl-slide-okabe-ito}

- Use blue, vermilion, bluish green and reddish purple for lines and points on
  white. Orange, sky blue and yellow need a dark outline or a dark background;
  a direct label does not raise their contrast. WCAG does exempt a mark that is
  not needed to read the data, so when every series carries a text label the
  line itself need not reach 3:1
  ([Understanding SC 1.4.11](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/non-text-contrast.html); @WCAG22:2023).
- Never use color as the only cue. Add a direct label, line type or marker
  shape, which is also what WCAG asks for [@WCAG22:2023].
- Avoid red against green. For a two-group contrast, pair vermilion with blue.

## Charts

Put the comparison that matters on a common scale. People read position along
a shared axis more accurately than length, angle or area
[@ClevelandMcGill:1984], and a crowdsourced replication preserved that ranking
[@HeerBostock:2010].

- **Pie charts.** Replace them with a sorted bar or dot chart, since angle and
  area are read less accurately than position. Keep a pie only for a two- or
  three-part share where the exact values are labeled.
- **Labels.** Label lines and bars directly at their ends instead of using a
  legend (spatial contiguity, above).
- **Highlight.** Draw the series or estimate that carries the message in a
  strong color and the rest in gray, and state it in the headline (signaling).
- **Strip.** Drop 3-D effects, background grids beyond light reference lines,
  and decoration (coherence).
- **Tables.** Convert to a figure when the point is a comparison. Keep a table
  only when the audience needs exact values, and cut it to the rows you will
  discuss.

## Directing attention

The eye finds a single item that differs in color, size or orientation within
about 200 to 250 ms, before the viewer has time to search [@HealeyEnns:2012].
Spend that on the one thing you want seen.

- **One pop-out per slide.** A single strong color or size difference marks
  the target; several compete for the same glance.
- **Hierarchy.** Headline largest, evidence next, labels smallest. Align
  elements to a grid and leave white space around the evidence.
- **Comparisons across slides.** Keep axes, scales and positions fixed when
  stepping between two figures. Viewers routinely miss changes they were not
  directed to ("change blindness", from the same review), so point to what
  changed.
- **Build-ups.** Add one layer per click and say what it adds (segmenting).

The hierarchy, grid and white-space advice is established design practice
rather than a tested effect. Treat it as a house convention, not a finding.

## What this changes from the older group rules

The group's slide rules go back to Blackstone's *Physiologic Approach to
Presentations* talk, the Research Day guides and the "Yahoo" slide templates.
The Yahoo rules themselves came from about three months of audience-response
and eye-tracking testing that Yahoo ran for the Cleveland Clinic, commissioned
by Toby Cosgrove (Eugene Blackstone, unpublished lecture, April 8, 2026). The
Yahoo report has not been found, so we cannot check its methods or its numbers.

Most of the rules hold up against the evidence above, and stay: nothing
extraneous, write the talk first, open and close with bookends, leave out
methods and statistics unless they are central, and convert tables to graphs.

What changes is narrower than it might look.

- **Sentence headlines** replace the one-line topic title.
- **Fewer bullets.** Prefer a figure; if bullets are needed, one level only.
  The old "no complete sentences" rule is revised rather than kept, because the
  problem is text that competes with your voice, not word count, and the
  headline itself is a sentence.
- **Direct labels** replace the hand-built legend.
- **Measured color contrast** replaces colors judged by eye. Check against
  4.5:1 and 3:1, and use Okabe-Ito for series.
- **Sorted bar or dot charts** replace pie charts.
- **16:9** is the standard; the 4:3 template is retired.
- **Background shading** (darker at the top, lighter at the bottom) is
  dropped. Yahoo's unpublished testing reportedly favored it, but we found no
  published evidence for it (see the checked claims at the end of this
  chapter).

The 32 pt minimum type size stays as a house rule, but read it as a house rule.
No study we found sets a minimum font size for a room. Fixed word limits such as
"7x7" are folklore with no evidence behind them; ask what work the slide asks
of the audience instead.

## Building the talk

This section and the three after it come from Dr. Eugene Blackstone's resident
education session on Research Day talks (unpublished lecture, April 8, 2026),
which updates his *Physiologic Approach to Presentations* deck. Its core
argument is the one this chapter opened with. A listener hears the talk once,
in order, cannot go back, and thinks faster than you speak, so the talk has to
keep listening easy. The sections above rest on published experiments; these
rest on experience at the podium. Where the two overlap, we say
how they fit.

1. **Know the frame.** Find out the time limit and the audience. Research Day
   is 6 minutes, enforced, and many national meetings allow 5. A mixed room of
   cardiac, thoracic and congenital surgeons shares little vocabulary, so
   define your terms and drop abbreviations and jargon.
2. **Write the message first.** Two or three sentences, usually your
   conclusions. A good abstract already contains the whole talk. The message
   sets the order, and anything that doesn't serve it comes out.
3. **Tell a story, not IMRD.** Introduction, methods, results, discussion is
   built for a reader who skips around strategically; a listener takes the talk
   serially. Reveal each piece just in time, so a method or an endpoint sits
   next to the result that needs it rather than in a methods block up front.
   It fits pre-training (@tbl-slide-mayer) as well: define a term before the
   result that uses it, and as close to that result as you can.
4. **Announce the structure and keep it.** If you say X, Y and Z, cover them
   in that order and use the same words for them every time.
5. **Chapters.** Turn each objective into a chapter with a one-second heading
   slide ("Early outcomes", then "Late outcomes"), so the audience always knows
   where they are. These are the section dividers that signaling asks for.
6. **Bookends.** Open by setting the context quickly, and close by returning to
   it with the clinical perspective. Use a motif in threes when it fits.
7. **End on the message, not a summary.** A 6-minute talk is already a
   summary. State the take-home message, then say "Thank you."

## Slide habits from the session

- **Pace, not slide count.** Plan on about 3 slides a minute, so at least a
  dozen for a 5-minute talk. A minute per slide means too much on each slide.
  What makes that pace possible is the Cosgrove rule, one idea per slide. Read
  it alongside "one task at a time" above: one idea is the default, and two
  ideas share a slide only when the relationship between them is the idea.
- **Slides support the talk.** They are not a script to read, and they need
  not be on all the time. A blank or black slide puts the attention back on
  you.
- **Meeting templates.** Use the meeting's template for the title and
  disclosure slides only. Drop watermarks and logos everywhere else, which is
  what coherence asks for too.
- **Room light sets the background.** Light background in a lit room, dark
  background in a dark room. Ask about the room before the meeting; it can
  change the day before. The contrast table above is measured against white, so
  check a dark-background deck against the same 4.5:1 and 3:1 thresholds.
- **Same place every time.** Keep titles, figures and labels in the same
  positions across slides so the eye knows where to land. Break the pattern
  only on purpose, such as a chapter heading.
- **Speak in reading order.** Lay the items out top to bottom and left to
  right, and present them in that order. Don't count on the eye following a
  fixed path, though; the session's scan order did not hold up (see the
  checked claims below). The headline and the highlight are what direct
  attention.
- **Orient first.** The first sentence on a new slide tells the audience how to
  read it ("Fungal is red, non-fungal is yellow"), before any result. That is
  pre-training at the scale of one slide.
- **Labels at full size.** Labels inside a figure (RCA, LCA) follow the same
  32 pt floor as the rest of the text.
- **Order follows the talk.** The charts section says to replace a pie with a
  sorted bar or dot chart. If you must keep a pie, order the slices the way you
  will discuss them, not largest to smallest.
- **Bar direction.** Consider horizontal bars with the category labels on the
  left when the labels are long. They fit, and each is read next to its bar.
  The claim that lay viewers read horizontal bars more easily did not hold up,
  so choose the direction for the labels, not for the audience.
- **No jumping slides.** Test the deck on the room's projector so the slides
  don't visibly jump between transitions. The Research Day team can help. A
  brief blank between slides hides the jump, but it also hides changes you
  want seen, so never put one between the steps of a build-up.
- **Images face into the slide.** A person in a photograph should look toward
  the slide's content or the other image, not off the edge.

## Delivery

Reading a short talk is fine. Most senior speakers do it because of the time
limits; what matters is that it doesn't sound read.

- **The speech box.** This is the presidential "blue box" format, used from
  FDR through Clinton. Every sentence is its own paragraph, in large type, with
  an arrow marking where it continues, and you slide each page down as you go.
  The group has four boxes to lend for Research Day.
- **Eyes up at both ends.** Look up at the start and at the end of each
  sentence, and down only in the middle. The audience reads that as speaking,
  and it slows you to a pace they can follow.
- **Voice.** Active and first person ("I did X; this is what I found"),
  semi-conversational, with energy and a good attitude. The audience is on your
  side.
- **Keep the audience in the present.** Pair ideas ("on the one hand ... on the
  other"), set up comparisons so they anticipate the result, pause or change
  pace to reset attention, and repeat the key point.
- **Face the audience, not the slides.** Keep a laser pointer steady; simple
  slides need none.

## Questions and answers

Treat the question period as part of the talk. Its purpose is to get the
message across again, and it is often the last impression people take away.
Research Day judges reward speakers who clearly know their work.

**Prepare.**

- Anticipate the questions with your sponsor and other knowledgeable people
  beforehand. You are not doing this alone.
- Know your study's limitations: what you did not study, and what you cannot
  conclude.
- Go in as the expert. On this subject, in this room, you know the data best.

**Avoid.**

- Answering with a paragraph when a sentence will do. It wanders off the
  message.
- Promissory notes ("we'll run that study and report back").
- Passing the question to your staff in the audience. If you don't know, say
  so and move on.
- Losing control to a hostile questioner.

**Steer back to the message.**

- Answer the question the questioner should have asked, ideally with something
  you already said, so the message repeats. Bridges such as "what may not be
  apparent here is ..." or "I'd like to return to what matters most" do this.
- **Silence.** If no one asks anything, ask yourself one ("You may be
  wondering ..."). It keeps the message going and often starts real questions.
- **Someone shares their own experience.** Thank them and tie it to your
  message.
- **A hostile question.** Correct a false statement plainly, use
  non-inflammatory words ("limitation", not "flaw"), skip sarcasm, and say only
  what you know to be true.

## Claims from the session, checked

Some of the advice above rests on specific claims, from the session or from
Yahoo's original testing, which has not been published. We checked each one
against published evidence. Most did not hold up as stated. The habits above
stay, adjusted where a claim they leaned on failed, and the claims stay out of
the evidence sections.

| Claim | Source | Verdict |
|--------------|------|------------------------|
| Speakers talk at about 114 words a minute while listeners think at about 300, leaving two-thirds of attention free | Session | Not supported as stated. It traces to [Nichols and Stevens (1957, *Harvard Business Review*, "Listening to People")](https://ombuds.columbia.edu/sites/default/files/content/pics/30%20Anniv/Listening%20to%20People.pdf), who give speech as about 125 words a minute and thought as "much higher"; the 300 and the two-thirds were added in retellings. Spare listening capacity is plausible but unmeasured. |
| Viewers scan a slide top to bottom, left to right, then clockwise | Yahoo eye tracking (unpublished) | Not supported. No Yahoo study was found. Eye tracking shows an F-shaped pattern only for unformatted text being skimmed, not a clockwise one, and headings and cues override it ([Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/f-shaped-pattern-reading-web-content/)). |
| Shading darker at the top and lighter at the bottom reads more easily | Yahoo audience response (unpublished) | No evidence found. Dropped. |
| Lay viewers read horizontal bar charts more easily than vertical ones | Session | Not supported. [Koesten and colleagues (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13713) found vertical bars rated more readable; earlier work is mixed. Horizontal bars are still useful for long labels. |
| Blue backgrounds keep audiences alert | Session | Not supported. The alerting effect of blue light comes from hours of intense short-wavelength light ([Cajochen and colleagues, 2005, *J Clin Endocrinol Metab* 90(3):1311](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15585546/)). No study has tested slide background color and alertness. |
| Pure black on white is fatiguing | Session | Not supported. Reading speed rises with contrast and then plateaus (Legge and colleagues, 1990, *J Opt Soc Am A* 7(10):2002), and dark text on a light ground beats the reverse for acuity and proofreading ([Piepenbrock and colleagues, 2013, *Ergonomics* 56(7)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23654206/)). Both are monitor studies, not projection. |
| Aptos reads more easily than Arial | Session | No evidence found. Aptos replaced Calibri as the Office default on design grounds. |
| A brief blank between slides hides the visible jump | Session | Partly supported. In Rensink, O'Regan and Clark (1997, *Psychological Science* 8:368-373), a change took about 11 s to spot with a blank between images and under 1 s without. A blank hides jumps, and it also hides changes you want seen. |

: Claims from the April 2026 session and the unpublished Yahoo testing, checked against published evidence. {#tbl-slide-claims tbl-colwidths="[28,14,58]"}

## Pitfalls

- **Reading the evidence as settled for your room.** The effect sizes above
  come mostly from students learning unfamiliar material, not clinicians at a
  conference. They are the best evidence available, and they are not a
  measurement of your audience.
- **Trusting a color-vision-safe palette for contrast.** Okabe-Ito separates
  hues for color-blind viewers; three of its seven colors still fall below 3:1
  on white.
- **Treating the font-size floor as a finding.** It is a sensible house rule
  with no study behind the number.
- **Citing session experience as evidence.** The habits from the session are
  experience, and worth following. Most of the specific claims behind them did
  not survive checking (@tbl-slide-claims), so don't quote them as findings.
